'''Sara Seager''' {{postnominals|country=CAN|OC}} (born July 21, 1971) is a Canadian-American [[astronomer]] and [[planetary science|planetary scientist]].<ref name="NYT-20161207">{{cite news|last=Jones|first=Chris|date=December 7, 2016|title=The Woman Who Might Find Us Another Earth|work=[[The New York Times Magazine]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/12/07/magazine/the-world-sees-me-as-the-one-who-will-find-another-earth.html|url-status=live|access-date=December 8, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210214062733/https://www.nytimes.com/2016/12/07/magazine/the-world-sees-me-as-the-one-who-will-find-another-earth.html|archive-date=February 14, 2021}}</ref> As of October 1, 2026 she is the North Star Distinguished Professor at her alma mater the [[University of Toronto]], in the [[Canadian Institute for Theoretical Astrophysics]] (CITA),<ref>{{Cite web |date=25 September 2026 |title=Incoming U of T professor Sara Seager named Eddie Goldenberg Distinguished Research Chair in Planetary and Molecular Sensing Technologies |url=https://www.chemistry.utoronto.ca/news/incoming-u-t-professor-sara-seager-named-eddie-goldenberg-distinguished-research-chair |access-date=24 October 2026 |publisher=Faculty of Arts & Science, University of Toronto}}</ref><ref name="UToronto" /> having previously spent 20 years as a professor at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=24 October 2026 |year=2026 |title=Sara Seager - Professor of Physics, Emerita (2006-2026) Class of 1941 Professor of Planetary Science, Emerita |url=https://physics.mit.edu/faculty/sara-seager/ |publisher=MIT Department of Physics}}</ref> Seager is known for her work on [[extrasolar planets]] and their atmospheres. She is the author of two textbooks on these topics,<ref>{{cite book |last=Seager |first=Sara |title=Exoplanet Atmospheres: Physical Processes |isbn=978-1-4008-3530-0 |date=2010 |publisher=Princeton University Press}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Seager |first=Sara |title=Exoplanets |isbn=978-0-8165-2945-2 |publisher=University of Arizona Press |date=2010}}</ref> and has been recognized for her ==Background==
Seager was born in [[Toronto]], Ontario, Canada, and is Jewish.<ref name="NYT-20161207" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Cohen|first=Anne|title=Four Jews Win MacArthur 'Genius' Awards|url=https://forward.com/news/breaking-news/184606/four-jews-win-macarthur-genius-awards/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201029233802/https://forward.com/news/breaking-news/184606/four-jews-win-macarthur-genius-awards/|archive-date=October 29, 2020|access-date=March 30, 2021|website=[[The Forward]]|date=September 27, 2013 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Dashefsky|first1=Arnold|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=CHV3BQAAQBAJ&pg=PA868|title=American Jewish Year Book 2014: The Annual Record of the North American Jewish Communities|last2=Sheskin|first2=Ira|publisher=Springer|year=2014|isbn=978-3-319-09623-0|page=868|access-date=June 10, 2017|archive-date=May 23, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200523045144/https://books.google.com/books?id=CHV3BQAAQBAJ&pg=PA868|url-status=live}}</ref> Her father, David Seager, who lost his hair when he was 19 years old, was a pioneer and one of the world's leaders in [[hair transplantation]] and the founder of the Seager Hair Transplant Centre in [[Toronto]].<ref name="NYT-20161207" /><ref>{{cite book|author=Michael D. Lemonick|title=Mirror Earth: The Search for Our Planet's Twin|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gjSWGMFkN8gC&pg=PT65|year=2012|publisher=Bloomsbury Publishing|isbn=978-0-8027-7902-1|page=65|access-date=June 10, 2017|archive-date=May 23, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200523045143/https://books.google.com/books?id=gjSWGMFkN8gC&pg=PT65|url-status=live}}</ref>

She earned her [[Bachelor of Science|BSc]] degree in mathematics and physics from the [[University of Toronto]] in 1994, assisted by a [[Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council|
NSERC University Undergraduate Student Research Award]], and a PhD in [[astronomy]] from [[Harvard University]] in 1999. Her doctoral thesis developed theoretical models of [[atmosphere]]s on extrasolar [[planet]]s and was supervised by [[Dimitar Sasselov]].<ref name=back/><ref name="SmithBaker2016"/><ref>{{cite thesis |bibcode=1999PhDT........18S |degree=PhD |publisher=Harvard University |first=Sara |last=Seager |title=Extrasolar giant planets under strong stellar irradiation |oclc=43085140 |date=1999|id={{ProQuest|304503987}} }}</ref>

She held a [[postdoctoral research]] fellow position at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] between 1999 and 2002 and a senior research staff member at the [[Carnegie Institution for Science|Carnegie Institution of Washington]] until 2006. She joined the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] in January 2007 as an associate professor in both physics and planetary science, was granted tenure in July 2007,<ref>{{cite news|date=November 14, 2007|title=MIT Corporation grants tenure to 50 faculty|publisher=MIT News Office|url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2007/tenure-tt1114.html|url-status=live|access-date=March 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200928034650/https://news.mit.edu/2007/tenure-tt1114|archive-date=September 28, 2020}}</ref> and was elevated to full professor in July 2010.<ref>{{cite news|date=December 29, 2010|title=Corporation announces faculty promotions and appointments|publisher=MIT News Office|url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2010/faculty-promotions-appointments.html|url-status=live|access-date=March 30, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200928034650/https://news.mit.edu/2007/tenure-tt1114|archive-date=September 28, 2020}}</ref> {{as of|2013}} she holds the "Class of 1941" chair.<ref name="CV" /> In November 2025, it was announced that Seager will join the Canadian Institute for Theoretical Astrophysics as North Star Distinguished Professor starting September 1, 2026.<ref name="UToronto">{{Cite news |date=November 12, 2025 |title=Renowned planetary scientist Sara Seager joins U of T and the Canadian Institute for Theoretical Astrophysics as North Star Distinguished Professor |url=https://www.artsci.utoronto.ca/news/renowned-planetary-scientist-sara-seager-joins-u-t-and-canadian-institute-theoretical |access-date=October 7, 2026 |work=Faculty of Arts & Science |language=en}}</ref>

She was elected a Legacy Fellow of the [[American Astronomical Society]] in 2020.

== Personal life ==
She is married to Charles Darrow and they have two sons from her first marriage. Her first spouse, Michael Wevrick, died of cancer in 2011.<ref>He also adopted her two children. {{cite web|last=Seager|first=Sara|date=January 14, 2013|title=So Many Exoplanets... So Few Women Scientists|url=http://www.huffingtonpost.com/sara-seager/women-in-science_b_2471980.html|access-date=September 25, 2013|work=[[The Huffington Post]]|archive-date=October 3, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131003092041/http://www.huffingtonpost.com/sara-seager/women-in-science_b_2471980.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|date=August 13, 2011|title=Obituary: Michael Wevrick|newspaper=[[Ottawa Citizen]]|url=http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/ottawacitizen/obituary.aspx?n=Michael-Wevrick&pid=153066177#fbLoggedOut|access-date=September 25, 2013|archive-date=September 27, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130927142116/http://www.legacy.com/obituaries/ottawacitizen/obituary.aspx?n=Michael-Wevrick&pid=153066177#fbLoggedOut|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |title=The Smallest Lights in the Universe: A Memoir, ''Sara Seager '', Crown, 2021, 336 pp |journal=Science |date=2026 |volume=393 |issue=6818 |page=1305 |doi=10.1126/science.aem0084 }}</ref>

==Academic research==
[[File:Sara Seager.webm|left|thumb|Seager talking about exoplanets]]
Seager's research has been primarily directed toward the discovery and analysis of [[exoplanets]]; in particular her work is centered around ostensibly rare [[earth analog]]s, leading [[NASA]] to dub her "an astronomical Indiana Jones."<ref>{{Cite web |first=Joshua |last=Rodriguez |title=On a quest for astronomy's holy grail |publisher=NASA |date=October 3, 2008 |url=https://exoplanets.nasa.gov/news/67/planet-hunters-on-a-quest-for-astronomys-holy-grail/ |access-date=June 12, 2017 |archive-date=February 19, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220219214443/https://exoplanets.nasa.gov/news/67/planet-hunters-on-a-quest-for-astronomys-holy-grail/ |url-status=live }}</ref> Seager used the term "gas dwarf" for a high-mass [[super-Earth]]-type planet composed mainly of [[hydrogen]] and [[helium]] in an animation of one model of the exoplanet [[Gliese 581c]]. The term "gas dwarf" has also been used to refer to planets smaller than [[gas giant]]s, with thick hydrogen and helium atmospheres.<ref>{{cite web|date=June 15, 2004|title=Of Gas Dwarfs and Waterworlds|url=http://216.231.48.101/forum/viewtopic.php?f=7&t=5228&start=0|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110704185304/http://216.231.48.101/forum/viewtopic.php?f=7&t=5228&start=0|archive-date=July 4, 2011|access-date=October 25, 2010|publisher=[[Celestia]] forum}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.eldacur.com/~brons/NerdCorner/StarGen/StarGen.html |title=StarGen – Solar System Generator |date=2003 |access-date=October 25, 2010 |archive-date=February 5, 2010 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100205065324/http://www.eldacur.com/~brons/NerdCorner/StarGen/StarGen.html |url-status=live }}</ref> Together with [[Marc Kuchner]], Seager had predicted the existence of [[carbon planet]]s.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Exoplanet Interior Composition |url=https://www.saraseager.com/exoplanet-interior-composition/ |access-date=February 26, 2024 |website=Sara Seager |language=en-US |archive-date=February 26, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240226054053/https://www.saraseager.com/exoplanet-interior-composition/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Seager has been the chair of the NASA Science and Technology Definition team for a proposed mission, "[[Starshade]]",<ref>Kramer, Miriam (March 24, 2014). "[https://www.space.com/25172-starshade-alien-earth-exoplanets-incredible-tech.html Incredible Technology: Giant Starshade Could Help Find an Alien Earth"], '' [[Space.com]]''. Retrieved 12 June 2023.</ref> to launch a free-flying [[occulting disk]], used to block the light from a distant star in order for a telescope to be able to resolve the (much dimmer) light from an accompanying exoplanet located in the habitable zone of the star.<ref>Grossman, Lisa (25 September 2013). "[https://www.newscientist.com/article/dn24247-nasa-revives-starshade-to-let-earth-like-worlds-shine/ NASA revives Starshade to let Earth-like worlds shine"], ''[[New Scientist]]''. Retrieved June 12, 2023.</ref>

In years since 2020, Sara has been focusing on work related to Venus, with the potential discovery of [[phosphine]], a [[biosignature]] gas, in the upper atmosphere.<ref>{{cite web|last=Anderson|first=Paul Scott|date=2020|title=Possible life signs in the clouds of Venus|url=https://earthsky.org/space/phosphine-disequilibrium-venus-atmosphere-pioneer-venus-1978|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210811113921/https://earthsky.org/space/phosphine-disequilibrium-venus-atmosphere-pioneer-venus-1978/|archive-date=August 11, 2021|access-date=August 26, 2021|website=[[EarthSky]]}}</ref>

===Seagers equation===
Seager developed a parallel version of the [[Drake equation]] to estimate the number of habitable planets in the Galaxy.<ref name="equation">{{Cite web|last=Powell|first=Devin|date=September 4, 2013|title=The Drake Equation Revisited: Interview with Planet Hunter Sara Seager|url=https://www.space.com/22648-drake-equation-alien-life-seager.html?cid=51463011558824|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210225062017/https://www.space.com/22648-drake-equation-alien-life-seager.html?cid=51463011558824|archive-date=February 25, 2021|access-date=March 30, 2021|website=[[Astrobiology Magazine]]}}</ref> Instead of aliens with radio technology, Seager has revised the [[Drake equation]] to focus on simply the presence of any alien life detectable from Earth. The equation focuses on the search for planets with biosignature gases, gases produced by life that can accumulate in a planet atmosphere to levels that can be detected with remote space telescopes.<ref name=equation />

: <math> N = N^*F_\text{Q} F_\text{HZ} F_\text{O} F_\text{L} F_\text{S} </math>

where:
* ''N'' = the number of planets with detectable signs of life
* ''N''* = the number of stars observed
* ''F''<sub>Q</sub> = the fraction of stars that are {{clarify|text=quiet|date=July 2026}}
* ''F''<sub>HZ</sub> = the fraction of stars with rocky planets in the habitable zone
* ''F''<sub>O</sub> = the fraction of stars with observable planets
* ''F''<sub>L</sub> = the fraction of planets that have life
* ''F''<sub>S</sub> = the fraction of life forms that produce planetary atmospheres with one or more detectable signature gases

===Asteria spacecraft===

Seager was the principal investigator of the [[ASTERIA (spacecraft)|Asteria]] (Arcsecond Space Telescope Enabling Research in Astrophysics) spacecraft,<ref>Seager, Sara (Jan/Feb. 2021). "[https://wp.technologyreview.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/12/MIT-NEWS-2021-01-1.pdf My satellite would fit in a small suitcase. But it could help us find other worlds]" (excerpt from book ''The Smallest Lights in the Universe'' (2020).) ''MIT News'', pp. 12–17. Retrieved May 20, 2023.</ref> a 6-U [[CubeSat|cubesat]] designed to do precision [[Photometry (astronomy)|photometry]] to search for extrasolar planets, a collaborative project between MIT and NASA's [[Jet Propulsion Laboratory]]. ASTERIA was launched into low Earth orbit from the [[International Space Station]] on November 20, 2017, and successfully operated until its orbital decay on April 24, 2020.

=== Venus missions ===
{{Primary sources section|date=March 2026}}
In 2020, Seager led a team proposing a mission ''[[Venus Life Finder]]'',<ref>{{cite web |date=December 10, 2021 |title=Venus Life Finder Mission Study |url=https://venuscloudlife.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/VLFReport_12092021.pdf |access-date=May 20, 2023 |work=Venus Cloud Life |publisher=[[MIT]] |pages=15–23 |archive-date=February 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240208215328/https://venuscloudlife.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/VLFReport_12092021.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> a small spacecraft to investigate the possibility of life in the atmosphere of Venus.<ref>{{cite web |date=December 10, 2021 |title="Newer, nimbler, faster:" Venus probe will search for signs of life in clouds of sulfuric acid |url=https://news.mit.edu/2021/newer-nimbler-faster-mission-venus-search-signs-life-clouds-sulfuric-acid-1210 |access-date=May 20, 2023 |work=[[MIT]]}}</ref> The mission will be a privately funded spacecraft to be launched by [[Rocket Lab]] on the [[Electron (rocket)|Electron]] rocket<ref>{{cite web |url=https://venuscloudlife.com/small-mission/ |title=Rocket Lab Probe |work=Venus Cloud Life |publisher=[[MIT]] |date=March 7, 2023 |access-date=April 10, 2023 |archive-date=February 8, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240208040505/https://venuscloudlife.com/small-mission/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> with a target launch date in summer 2026.<ref name="w409">{{cite web | title=Rocket Lab Mission to Venus | website=Venus Missions|url=https://www.morningstarmissions.space/rocketlabmissiontovenus | access-date=February 28, 2025}}</ref>

The Morning Star Missions to Venus team, including Seager, have planned a thorough list of missions with the aim of finding "signs of life or life itself" on Venus.<ref name="Iakubivskyi">Iakubivskyi, I., Seager, S., Carr, C.E. ''et al.'' Venus cloud catcher as a proof of concept aerosol collection instrument. ''Sci Rep'' '''14''', 30045 (2024). <nowiki>https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-024-80847-8</nowiki></ref>  These missions include the Venus Habitability Mission, Rocket Lab Mission to Venus, and Atmospheric Cloud Sample Return Mission.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Space Scroll Animation Design {{!}} Wix Studio |url=https://www.morningstarmissions.space/ |access-date=March 16, 2026 |website=Venus Morning Star Missions |language=en}}</ref>  The feasibility of these missions depends on the efficiency of atmospheric data collection, through the direct in-situ examination of collected cloud liquid material, or the sample return of the material with further investigation to be performed on Earth-based laboratories.<ref name="Iakubivskyi" /> The proposed instrumentation include cost-effective probes designed to investigate the chemical signatures and will return solid, liquid, and cloud samples from the 48&nbsp;km to 60&nbsp;km altitude cloud-decks of Venus.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Atmospheric Sample Return Mission |url=https://www.morningstarmissions.space/samplereturnmission |access-date=March 16, 2026 |website=Venus Missions |language=en}}</ref> The mission schedule for the Venus Habitability Mission is set with a target launch date of May 2031.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Venus Habitability Mission |url=https://www.morningstarmissions.space/venushabitabilitymission |access-date=March 16, 2026 |website=Venus Missions |language=en}}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==
Seager was awarded the 2012 [[Sackler Prize]] for "analysis of the atmospheres and internal compositions of extra-solar planets,"<ref>{{cite news |url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2012/seager-sackler-prize.html |title=Sara Seager Named Co-Winner of the 2012 Sackler Prize |publisher=MIT News Office |date=April 18, 2012 |access-date=September 25, 2013 |archive-date=April 4, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130404032547/http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2012/seager-sackler-prize.html |url-status=live }}</ref> the [[Helen B. Warner Prize for Astronomy|Helen B. Warner Prize]] from the [[American Astronomical Society]] in 2007 for developing "fundamental techniques for understanding, analyzing, and finding the atmospheres of extrasolar planets,"<ref>{{cite web |url=http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2007/seager-award.html |title=Helen B. Warner Prize |date=February 5, 2007 |publisher=[[American Astronomical Society]] |access-date=April 11, 2007 |archive-date=February 8, 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070208144334/http://web.mit.edu/newsoffice/2007/seager-award.html |url-status=live }}</ref> and the 2004 Harvard Book Prize in Astronomy.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://astronomy.fas.harvard.edu/book/bok-prize-recipients |title=Bok Prize Recipients |publisher=[[Harvard University]] Department of Astronomy |access-date=December 12, 2012 |archive-date=May 15, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120515144925/http://astronomy.fas.harvard.edu/book/bok-prize-recipients |url-status=live }}</ref> She was appointed as a fellow to the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 2012 and elected to the [[Royal Astronomical Society of Canada]] as an honorary member in 2013.<ref name="CV" /> In September 2013 she became a [[MacArthur Fellows Program|MacArthur Fellow]].<ref>{{Cite web|date=September 15, 2013|title=Sara Seager: Astrophysicist {{!}} Class of 2013|url=https://www.macfound.org/fellows/903/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190904083531/https://www.macfound.org/fellows/903/|archive-date=September 4, 2019|access-date=September 13, 2019|website=[[MacArthur Foundation]]}}</ref> She was elected to the [[American Philosophical Society]] in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.amphilsoc.org/blog/election-new-members-2018-spring-meeting|title=Election of New Members at the 2018 Spring Meeting|website=American Philosophical Society|access-date=June 2, 2018|archive-date=December 23, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191223042357/https://www.amphilsoc.org/blog/election-new-members-2018-spring-meeting|url-status=live}}</ref> She was the Elizabeth R. Laird Lecturer at [[Memorial University of Newfoundland]] in 2018.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gazette.mun.ca/public-engagement/holy-grail/|title=Holy Grail|last=Foss|first=Kelly|date=September 20, 2018|website=Gazette – Memorial University of Newfoundland|language=en-CA|access-date=July 7, 2019|archive-date=July 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190707223423/https://gazette.mun.ca/public-engagement/holy-grail/|url-status=live}}</ref> On August 19, 2020, Seager appeared on the ''[[Lex Fridman#Lex Fridman Podcast|Lex Fridman Podcast]]'' (#116).<ref>{{Cite web|date=August 16, 2020|title=#116 – Sara Seager: Search for Planets and Life Outside Our Solar System|url=https://lexfridman.com/sara-seager/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201024002444/https://lexfridman.com/sara-seager/|archive-date=October 24, 2020|access-date=April 1, 2021|website=Lex Fridman}}</ref>

In 2020, she was appointed as an Officer of the [[Order of Canada]].<ref>{{cite web|date=November 27, 2020|title=Governor General Announces 114 New Appointments to the Order of Canada|url=https://www.gg.ca/en/activities/2020/governor-general-announces-114-new-appointments-order-canada|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210123071759/https://www.gg.ca/en/activities/2020/governor-general-announces-114-new-appointments-order-canada|archive-date=January 23, 2021|access-date=March 30, 2021|website=[[Governor General of Canada]]}}</ref> She won the 2020 [[Los Angeles Times Book Prize for Science and Technology|''Los Angeles Times'' Prize for Science and Technology]] for ''The Smallest Lights in the Universe.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Pineda|first=Dorany|date=April 17, 2021|title=Winners of the 2020 L.A. Times Book Prizes announced|url=https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/books/story/2021-04-16/winners-of-the-2020-l-a-times-book-prizes-announced|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210417011609/https://www.latimes.com/entertainment-arts/books/story/2021-04-16/winners-of-the-2020-l-a-times-book-prizes-announced|archive-date=April 17, 2021|access-date=April 17, 2021|website=[[Los Angeles Times]]|language=en-US}}</ref>''

She was an honorary graduand at her alma mater, the [[University of Toronto]] Spring 2023 Convocation.<ref>{{Cite web|date=June 15, 2023|title=Spring 2023 Convocation|url=https://governingcouncil.utoronto.ca/convocation/ceremonies?page=2}}</ref>

In 2024, Seager was awarded the [[Kavli Prize]] in Astrophysics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Home |url=https://www.kavliprize.org/?et_cid=5243269 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240612164453/https://www.kavliprize.org/?et_cid=5243269 |archive-date=June 12, 2024 |access-date=June 12, 2024 |website=www.kavliprize.org}}</ref>

Sara Seager received the 2025 Nomis Distinguished Scientist and Scholar Award. 

The NOMIS Foundation connects the award to her project on habitability and the search for life beyond Earth.<ref>{{Cite web |title=NOMIS Award |url=https://nomisfoundation.ch/research/nomis-award/ |access-date=23 October 2026 |website=NOMIS Foundation}}</ref>
